# Surface

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

What shape does a landscape have, sampled on a grid? `surface` draws a sheet
through your samples. It is a sheet through *three* positions: x, y and a
height. The height comes from a column bound to `z` or from a transform, and
without it there is no sheet at all. That makes it the only mark that *must* be
drawn in the [cube](../space.qmd), where a third axis carries the height. Every
other mark draws in the plane. Six of them can also draw in the cube: `point`,
`bar`, `interval`, `box`, `text` and `path`.

It is not [`area`](area.qmd) with a `z`. An area fills the space between a curve
and a baseline. A surface has no baseline. Both are fills, and that is all they
share.

## A sheet through the samples {#a-sheet-through-the-samples}

A grid of elevations is a table of numbers. Nobody can see a hill in a column of
numbers. Draw the same numbers as a sheet and the hill appears. Here is Maunga
Whau, a volcano in Auckland. The original grid has a sample every 10 m. The
book's copy keeps every second sample in each direction, so its 1364 samples are
20 m apart. Ross Ihaka digitized the elevations from a topographic map, and R's
`datasets` package is where the book reads them [@rcore2026]:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(maunga_whau)
```

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, at 20 m")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation."*

Three positions and a mark. There is no `space()` in that sentence and none is
needed: binding `z` is what puts a plot in the cube, exactly as it is for a [3-D
scatter](../space.qmd). A bare `space()` draws the same plot. Write
`space(turn =, tilt =)` when you want a different angle. `z_label()` names the third axis, the way `x_label()`
names the first, and [Space](../space.qmd#z_label-naming-the-third-axis)
explains it.

## One row per crossing {#one-row-per-crossing}

What shape must a table have before a surface can draw it? A scatter's table
does not have that shape, and knowing why tells you which of your tables can
become a sheet. Given two position columns and no transform, a surface reads
each row as a **crossing**: the point where one `x` value meets one `y` value.
Between four neighboring crossings, gog draws one **face**, a small four-sided
piece of the sheet. A [`zone`](zone.qmd) also fills a rectangle, but a flat one,
and shows its value by color. Each corner of a face is at its crossing's height,
so a face can slope. The grid those faces make is the sheet's **mesh**. You never
declare which crossings are neighbors. gog finds them from your two position
columns: the distinct `x` values and the distinct `y` values (here `east` and
`north`) become the **mesh lines**, one set in each direction. A **cell**
is the rectangle between two neighboring mesh lines in each direction, and a
face is drawn wherever all four corners of a cell are present.

So this reading needs a table with one row per (x, y) crossing: every `x` value
paired with every `y` value.

Maunga Whau has that shape. It holds 1364 rows, 31 distinct `east` values and 44
distinct `north` values: 31 × 44 = 1364, so the grid is full, and 30 × 43 = 1290
faces get drawn.

The same count shows why a scatter cannot be a surface. The gapminder 2007 table
below holds 142 countries, and no two of them share a `gdp` value or a `life`
value. That makes a grid 142 wide and 142 deep holding only 142 crossings, so no
cell has all four corners. The sheet would be empty:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + surface + x(gdp) + y(life) + z(population)
```

That refusal names the two sentences that *do* draw: a `point` with a `z` to
draw each country, and `surface * density` for a **field** estimated from those
points. A field is one value at every place on the plane. [The third geometry of
one field](#the-third-geometry-of-one-field) draws `surface * density` for the
iris flowers.

Because a face needs all four of its corners, a gap in the grid is an
**opening** in the sheet rather than a face drawn across it. The `peak` table is
Maunga Whau with the crossings around the summit dropped. The sheet opens there
rather than covering the gap:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(peak)
```

```{r}
#| message: true
data(peak) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("A gap in the grid, left open")
```

*"Given the peak table: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation."*

The note above the plot counts the crossings gog did find: 1322 of 1364, so 42
crossings are missing. Each missing crossing removes every face that needed it,
so more than 42 faces are missing: 1234 are drawn here, where the full grid
draws 1290. The note is advice rather than a refusal, because a grid with gaps
is a legitimate thing to have and a sheet with openings is a true picture of
one. What would not be legitimate is quietly spanning a gap, which claims a
height nobody measured. The note also says what to check if you expected a whole
sheet: each position value must repeat exactly. If one row holds 1.2 and another
1.2000001, gog makes two mesh lines where you meant one, and the sheet gets
openings you did not intend.

## A continuous floor {#a-continuous-floor}

Some tables hold a category in one column, such as a continent, and a number in
another, such as a year. Every continent is paired with every year, so the rows
form a grid, and a sheet over them seems reasonable. The two position columns make
the sheet's **floor**, the plane under it, and both have to be continuous. A face
stretches from one sample to the next and so claims every height *between* them,
and between one category and the next there is nothing to claim. So a category
on either position is refused.

Numbers cut into cells are different, and a surface takes those, as [When each
cell holds one value](#when-each-cell-holds-one-value) shows. Cut cells meet
edge to edge, and the edge between two cells is itself a number on the axis.
A category instead owns a **slot**, a share of the axis that is its own, and the
line between two slots stands for no value at all. So gog draws a surface over
cells cut from numbers, and refuses it over the slots of categories. The flat marks show the same difference: bars over
categories have gaps between them, and the bars of a histogram touch.

The refusal, shown in [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses), names the mark that
does take a category on both positions: the [3-D
bar](../space.qmd#transforms-in-the-cube). A 3-D bar is *in* its slot and
claims nothing about the space between slots. The `gm_eras` table has two rows
for each of 142 countries, one for 1957 and one for 2007. The year is in two
columns: `year` holds it as a number, and `era` holds it as a category. With
`continent` on `x` and `era` on `y`, both floor positions hold a category. The
refusal's message writes `bar * count`, which counts rows. This table has a
measurement, so `bar * mean` averages `life`, bound to `z`, for each continent
in each era. `style(gap = 0.5)` leaves half of each slot empty, so the space
between the bars is easy to see:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_eras)
```

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) +
  style(gap = 0.5)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is era, z is
life, with gap 0.5."*

In every continent the 2007 bar is taller than the 1957 one, and Asia's rose
the most, from 49 to 71 years. A surface cannot be drawn over these slots: the
bars have empty space between them, and a sheet has none.

## The third geometry of one field {#the-third-geometry-of-one-field}

Which of two clusters of flowers is denser, and by how much? The `iris_flowers`
table holds 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species. With petal length on
`x` and sepal length on `y`, they form two clusters: setosa alone, and the other
two species together. A heatmap and a contour plot, the first two plots below,
show where each cluster is. To find how dense it is, you have to read a legend
or a contour level. Two transforms tile a floor under a surface, `bin` and
`density`. With `density`, a surface becomes the third way gog draws a field.
The same estimate over the same two columns, three times:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + title("As cells: zone")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is petal length, y is
sepal length."*

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + path * density +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + title("As contours: path")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density, x is petal length, y is
sepal length."*

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + surface * density +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space(turn = 120) +
  title("As a sheet: surface")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: a surface derived by density, x is petal length, y is
sepal length, in the cube, turned 120."*

The sheet is turned to 120 degrees because of where the two peaks are. They are
on a diagonal of the floor. At the default angle the near peak is directly in
front of the far one and hides it, so the sheet shows one peak where the data
has two. [One sheet, four angles](#one-sheet-four-angles) returns to that,
because every 3-D view has this problem, not only this one.

All three plots say the same thing about these two clusters: they are nearly
equally dense at their centers. The cluster with long petals is the denser one,
by about four percent. What each plot asks of the reader is different. In the
cells you compare two shades against a legend. In the contours you count rings.
On the sheet you compare two heights, and that needs no legend at all. Which of
the three you want depends on what you are asking, not on which mark is better.

One transform, three marks, and the estimate itself is the same in all three.
What differs is where each mark puts the measurement. A `zone` puts it in color.
A `path` puts it in the level each contour was cut at. A surface puts it in
*height*. That is why the third sentence never binds `z()` and still gets a
third axis, labeled Density. The transform supplies the measurement, and the
mark puts it on the height. A flat `bar * bin` does the same for `y`.

| Mark derived by `density`, over two positions | Where the measurement goes |
|---|---|
| `zone * density` | into the color of each cell |
| `path * density` | into the level each contour was cut at |
| `surface * density` | into the height of the sheet, the third plot above |

Here the transform stays the same, and each mark supplies its own geometry. So
gog has no separate atom for a contour plot or a density heatmap: each is
`density` drawn by a different mark.

The sheet is computed on the same grid as the heatmap's cells: 64 places along
each axis, so 63 × 63 cells. Each cell is drawn as a flat top, and each step
between two cells as a vertical face. The steps are too small to see
separately, so the sheet looks smooth. [When each cell holds one
value](#when-each-cell-holds-one-value) shows such steps on larger cells, where
they are easy to see. `density(places = )` changes the number of places, and
the plot's file grows with the square of `places`. This sheet's file is about
1.6 MB at the default, three times the heatmap's, because gog draws nearly
three faces for each cell. At 128 places it is about 6.5 MB,
and at 256, the most places a field allows, about 26 MB. Fewer places draw a coarser sheet in a smaller
file. [How many
places](../transforms.qmd#how-many-places-places) lists the default of every
reading of `density`.

The `surface * density` sentence above writes `space()`, and the chapter's first
sentence, for the volcano, did not. A bound `z` can mean only one thing: the
table has three columns to place on positions. When a transform computes the
measure, gog knows only that the layer has one, not which axis it goes on.
`density` computes that measure in the plane too, where it becomes a color, so
`space()` is what tells gog to put it on a third axis. Leave `space()` out, and
gog refuses the sentence, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

## When each cell holds one value {#when-each-cell-holds-one-value}

The volcano's sheet joins its samples with sloping faces. Does the ground rise
smoothly between your samples, or does each cell hold one value that says
nothing about its neighbors? `bin` is the other transform that tiles a floor. It
cuts the floor into cells, and `mean` gives each cell the average elevation of
the rows inside it. The surface is then flat across each cell, with a step at
each boundary. The density sheet above is drawn the same way, from much smaller
cells. Here is the same volcano, read as a coarse grid rather than a fine one:

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is east, y is
north, z is elevation."*

Nothing about the volcano changed. What changed is the **claim**. The sheet at
the top of this chapter says the ground rises smoothly between its samples. This
one gives each cell one elevation, the mean of its samples, and says nothing
about how the ground varies inside the cell. Each claim is right for a different
kind of data, and which one you want is a question about how yours was measured.

That question has a clear answer in an experiment or a simulation, where the
conditions form a grid with exactly one number in each cell. Read as crossings,
such a table gives fewer faces than it has values. Nine values make a 3 × 3 grid
of crossings. A face needs four crossings at its corners, so the sheet has
2 × 2 = 4 faces, and no face stands for any one value:

```{r}
cells <- data.frame(
  a = c(-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2),
  b = c(-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2),
  v = c(0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039)
)

data(cells) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) + title("Nine values, four faces")
```

*"Given the cells: a surface, x is a, y is b, z is v."*

Nine numbers became four faces, and each face slopes between the four values at
its corners. Cut the floor into cells instead, and each cell gets a flat top of
its own, a **plateau**:

```{r}
data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
  color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus")
```

*"Given the cells: a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z
is v, color by v, with the plasma palette."*

Nine plateaus, and three colors. The nine values make a symmetric bowl: the four
corner cells share the highest value, the four edge cells share the middle one,
and the center cell holds the lowest. The ramp makes that symmetry visible. In
the plain sheet above, you had to read the symmetry from the axis.

A 3-D bar uses the same sentence: `bin` cuts the `x` and `y` axes into cells, and
`mean` averages the column named on `z` inside each one. The transforms mean the
same thing on both marks, and only the geometry laid on the cell differs. Here
`mean` does no averaging, because this table holds one row per cell. It is still
needed: without it, `bin` counts the rows in each cell, so `z(v)` would name a
column the plot never reads, and gog refuses the sentence.

The step between two plateaus is drawn as a **vertical face** along the line the
two cells share. That line has no width, so the vertical face claims nothing
about any area: it is simply what a jump looks like. Vertical faces keep the
plateaus joined at every step, so a gap in the sheet always means a missing
cell.

A vertical face spans the *difference* between two neighbors, and a [3-D
bar](../space.qmd#transforms-in-the-cube) on every cell does not. A bar always reaches down to the floor
of the cube, so a grid of bars hides its own back rows as soon as you turn it. A vertical
face is only as tall as its own step. The next plot turns both to 60 degrees, so
you can see which one is still legible. Both are set to one color, so the only
thing that differs between them is the shape:

```{r}
((data(cells) + bar * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
    space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
   (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
      space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Plateaus, turned"))) +
  theme(height = 430)
```

*"Given the cells: bars derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v,
turned 60, beside a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is
v, turned 60."*

`|` composes them ([Composition](../composition.qmd)), so the two are one
figure and turn together. That is what makes this a fair comparison, rather
than two pictures the reader has to match angle by angle.

`theme(height = )` sets the whole arrangement's height in pixels. It is set here
because two cubes side by side each get half its width but the full height, so
each panel is tall and narrow. A cube keeps its proportions, so it never stretches
to fill a tall panel. Without the setting, blank
space would be left above and below each cube.

gog has no special rule for empty cells. `bin` leaves them out, because a cell
with no rows is not a measurement of zero. A plateau claims only its own cell,
so a cell with nothing in it is simply a cell with no top. It is the same
opening a missing crossing makes in the mesh, for a different reason.

What a surface refuses is a grid of slots, the cells two categories make. [What
it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows that refusal.

## The mesh, and what the shading means {#the-mesh-and-what-the-shading-means}

A smooth sheet hides where its samples were. A
[line](line.qmd#layering-a-line-over-other-marks) hides its measurements the
same way, and a dot at each row shows them again. On a surface, the mesh lines show the
grid again, so a reader can see how fine the sampling was. `border_color` and `border_size` draw them. A face is a
closed-shape fill, like a bar or a box, so the [settable
rule](../design-laws.qmd#the-settable-rule) gives it a border. On a surface,
those borders are the mesh lines:

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, with
border color white and border size 0.4."*

The mesh lines add no shapes to the picture, because every face is already
stroked in its own shade. That thin stroke covers the pale seam that would
otherwise show between neighboring faces. `border_color` replaces the stroke's
color, and `border_size` its width. Leave both out for a seamless sheet. A
`border_size` of 0 removes the stroke, and the pale seams appear.

Look at the shading on the sheet above, and on the turned one below it. The faces
are shaded by their **slope**: a steep one is darker, a flat one keeps its full
color. That is a fact about the terrain, not about where a light is, so turning
the scene rearranges the faces on the page and repaints none of them:

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  space(turn = 130, tilt = 35) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Turned, with the same shades")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, turned
130, tilted 35."*

Compare the crater walls here with the first plot, in [A sheet through the
samples](#a-sheet-through-the-samples). The faces and their shades are the same,
seen from another side. A shade comes from the slope alone, so it stays the
same at every angle. This sheet has one color, so a darker face is always a
steeper one.

## Color by height, per face {#color-by-height-per-face}

Slope shading says how steep a face is, not how high it is. How high is the
summit, and how deep is the crater? `color` maps on a surface, and a
*continuous* column colors it face by face along a ramp.
[`palette()`](../style.qmd#palette-choosing-the-colors-a-mapping-uses) chooses
which ramp. `"viridis"` suits a topographic sheet, because it gets steadily
lighter from its lowest color to its highest:

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + color(elevation) +
  palette("viridis") +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by
elevation, with the viridis palette."*

Compare that with the chapter's first plot, in [A sheet through the
samples](#a-sheet-through-the-samples). The summit and the crater rim are in
that plot too. With slope shading alone you have to infer them from which
faces are dark. The ramp states the heights, and the legend decodes them.

Mapping the height to color when `z` already shows it is redundant on purpose.
It is what a reader of a topographic map expects. It also shows why a surface
can take a continuous color when an [`area`](area.qmd) cannot. An area is one
region with one color. A continuous column would change the color inside that
region, so `color` on an `area` refuses one. A surface has *faces*, and a face
is small enough to hold one value.

A face has four corners and one color. Its color is the mean of its four corner
values, which stands for the field at its center. So the ramp describes the mesh
you have, not only the field you sampled from. Here is one bowl-shaped field,
sampled coarsely and then finely. Its value `v` is lowest at the center, where
`a` and `b` are both 0, and rises the same way toward every edge. The `coarse`
table samples it on a 3 by 3 grid, and the `fine` table on a 7 by 7 grid:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(coarse)
peek(fine)
```

```{r}
((data(coarse) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
    color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Sampled 3 by 3: four faces")) |
   (data(fine) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
      color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Sampled 7 by 7: thirty-six faces"))) +
  theme(height = 320)
```

*"Given coarse: a surface, x is a, y is b, z is v, color by v, with the plasma
palette, beside the same given fine."*

This figure draws from two tables, `coarse` and `fine`. gog finds each plot's
table by the name `data()` records, so two different tables in one figure need
two different names ([Two tables with one
name](../bindings/r.qmd#two-tables-with-one-name)).

The left sheet is one uniform color, and that is correct rather than broken.
Every face has one high corner, one low corner and two middle ones, so all four
faces get the same average. The mesh is too coarse to hold the shape, and the
ramp says so instead of inventing a gradient across it. The right sheet has the
same field under it and enough faces to resolve it, so the bowl appears.

This is the reading that makes the legend trustworthy. A color is the height at
one stated place, the center of a face, so two faces of one color really are at
one height there, and a sheet of one color has all its face centers at one
height.

The ramp does not replace the slope shading. A face takes its color from the
ramp and is then darkened by how steep it is, so a steep face with a dark
color gets darker still. Viridis gives its dark colors only to the *low*
ground, and low ground is usually flat, so few faces are both dark and steep.

An estimated height takes a ramp the same way, and you name it the same way.
`density` writes its estimate into a column called `density`, so `density` is
the name you give `color`, exactly as on a [`zone`](zone.qmd). On a
[`path`](path.qmd), `density` writes the estimate into a column called `level`
instead, one value for each ring. Here the sheet shows the estimate as a height
and as a ramp. The plot uses the `iris_flowers` table, shown in [The third
geometry of one field](#the-third-geometry-of-one-field):

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + surface * density +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space() + color(density) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The estimate, as a height and as a ramp")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: a surface derived by density, x is petal length, y is
sepal length, in the cube, color by density, with the viridis palette."*

Nothing there is a special case. The transform writes a column, the column has a
name, and a name can be bound. Whether the height came from your table or from
an estimate is only a difference in source. It does not change what you may say
about it.

Whether you *want* the color as well as the height is a separate question. The
plain sheet in [A sheet through the samples](#a-sheet-through-the-samples)
already shows the height by position alone. Use the ramp when the low ground
matters. Slope shading darkens a steep face but not a flat one, so a broad, low
mound and the flat ground around it are drawn almost the same color. The ramp is
what separates them.

Sometimes faces belong to named parts of the ground rather than to heights. A
*categorical* color gives each face the color of its category. Unlike on a
`line`, it does not split the rows: the sheet stays one sheet, and only `group`
makes separate sheets. The `band` table is Maunga Whau with one more column,
`side`: `north half` where `north` is greater than 440, and `south half` for the
rest:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(band)
```

```{r}
data(band) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + color(side) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Two halves, one sheet")
```

*"Given the band table: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color
by side."*

The two colors meet between the crossings at 440 and 460 meters north, and the
sheet has no gap there. A face whose corners hold both categories takes the
category of its corner with the smallest `east` and `north`, so the faces between
440 and 460 belong to the south half. To draw a separate sheet for each category,
use `group`, as the next section shows.

## Two sheets over one floor {#two-sheets-over-one-floor}

What if one table holds the heights of two sheets over the same floor? The
`crop_response` table is invented for this book. It gives a wheat yield, in
metric tons per hectare, for two varieties of wheat, a hardy one and a
high-yield one. Nitrogen fertilizer runs from 0 to 200 kilograms per hectare
and water from 100 to 500 millimeters, six amounts of each.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(crop_response)
```

Each crossing holds two rows, one for each variety. A sheet has one height at
each crossing, so gog refuses to draw the table as one sheet:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(crop_response) + surface + x(nitrogen) + y(water) + z(yield)
```

The message names the column that splits the rows.

[`group(variety)`](../channels.qmd#group) draws one sheet for each variety.
`group` splits without coloring, so `color(variety)` gives each sheet its own
color:

```{r}
data(crop_response) + surface + x(nitrogen) + y(water) + z(yield) +
  group(variety) + color(variety) +
  z_label("Yield (t/ha)") + title("Two varieties over one floor")
```

*"Given the crop response: surfaces, x is nitrogen, y is water, z is yield,
grouped by variety, color by variety."*

The two sheets cross. The hardy variety yields more where nitrogen or water is
low, and the high-yield variety yields more where both are high. gog draws the
faces of both sheets in one depth sort, farthest first, as it draws a [path's
segments](path.qmd#a-path-in-the-cube). It does not draw one sheet and then the
other. Each face takes its own place in that order, so the picture shows each
sheet passing through the other where they cross.

## Opacity by a measure, per face {#opacity-by-a-measure-per-face}

A color decides what a face says. An opacity decides whether you can see
through it. Part of a sheet is often not the subject. The flat ground around a
hill only hides what is behind it, and fading those faces makes the hill the
solid part of the picture. `opacity` maps on a surface, and it maps for the
reason `color` does. A face is small enough to hold one value, so it can hold an
opacity too. Every face takes its own opacity, and a face fades where its
measure is small:

```{r}
data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + opacity(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Faint where the ground is low")
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, opacity
by elevation."*

Over the low ground the fill fades to almost nothing and each face keeps its
outline, so that part of the sheet shows as mesh lines alone. A ramp cannot do
that; an opacity can. The legend beside the plot reads the same way `color`'s
does, with the smallest, middle and largest values of the column.

No face disappears completely. A mapped `opacity` runs from 0.15 to 0.95, so the
faintest face here is still drawn, which is the rule every mapped `opacity`
follows ([Channels](../channels.qmd#opacity)).

A face reads its opacity the way it reads its color, from the mean of its four
corners. A plateau reads its own cell's row. A vertical face is between two
cells and reads the taller one's row, the way a bar's side takes the bar's
color. Either way one face has one reading, whichever channel asks for it.

The sentence behind the first plot in this section binds `elevation` twice: once
to `z` and once to `opacity`. A second column is the more useful case: the shape
stays in `z`, and another measure decides which faces fade. The `relief` table
is Maunga Whau with one more column, `steepness`: how much the elevation changes
toward the next crossing east and the next crossing north, combined:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(relief)
```

```{r}
data(relief) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + opacity(steepness) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Solid where the ground is steep")
```

*"Given the relief table: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation,
opacity by steepness."*

The steep sides of the hill stay solid, and the flat ground around them fades away. The sheet is the same
shape as the one above it, and a different part of it is solid.

An [`area`](area.qmd) refuses a mapped opacity, from a categorical column as
well as a continuous one. An area takes one opacity for the whole layer, so no
row can change it. A surface has faces, and each face can carry its own color
and its own opacity.

One value for the whole sheet is still [`style(opacity = )`](../style.qmd). Set
it when you want to see one sheet through another, and map it when you want each
face to fade by its own value.

## One sheet, four angles {#one-sheet-four-angles}

A still 3-D plot hides something at every angle, and which thing it hides
depends on the angle you pick. So turn the same sheet rather than trust one view
of it. Each of the other three changes exactly *one* of `turn`/`tilt` from the
default view at the top left:

```{r}
((data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 30, tilt = 25) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The default view")) |
 (data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 140, tilt = 25) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Turned: the same sheet from the west"))) /
((data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 30, tilt = 70) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Tilted up: the crater appears")) |
 (data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 30, tilt = 5) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Tilted down: the view from the side")))
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by
elevation, with the viridis palette, turned 30, tilted 25, beside the same
turned 140; above the same tilted 70, beside the same tilted 5."*

Read them as a set and you can see what each angle hides. The crater is the most
interesting thing about this hill, and the two plots in the top row do not show it. The
rim nearest you is in front of the crater, so turning alone does not show it
while the tilt is low. Tilt up and you can see into the crater, because you are
now looking down from above. The same tilt flattens the heights, until the sheet
looks like a flat colored map. Tilt down instead and you get the opposite: the
heights read clearly, the view from above is gone, and the sheet shows as an
outline. One or the other, never both.

These four plots show why you would want to turn a plot. Here you need both the
view from above and the view from the side, and no single still view shows this
hill whole. So, in the web edition, turn the four with the pointer. Raise the tilt until the
crater appears, and watch the heights flatten as the tilt rises. The four still
views show the problem, and dragging lets you see every angle between them.

All four turn together, because `|` and `/` composed them into one figure. Each
panel keeps the angle its own sentence asked for, and the drag adds the same
change to every one. The *reset* button returns each to the angle it opened at. To turn one alone,
write it alone.

That is composition rather than faceting, and the two share the same pair of
operators. A facet names a *column* ([Faceting](../faceting.qmd)), and a viewing
angle is not a column: it is a property of the coordinate space, the way a
`polar()` start angle is. gog does build small multiples of cubes, one cube for
each value of a column, but these four panels are not small multiples.
[Space](../space.qmd#faceting-one-cube-per-panel) has that example.

One limit shows in these four plots, and it belongs to the cube rather than to
the mark. Notice the Elevation axis in the tilted-up panel. You are looking down
along it, so it is drawn at about a third of its full length. gog labels three
heights on that axis, while the default view, top left, labels five. gog leaves
numbers out rather than let them overlap. [Space](../space.qmd) says which numbers a crowded
axis drops, and why the scale itself never changes.

## What a surface is for {#what-a-surface-is-for}

A surface is for anything that is a *height over a plane*. Terrain, and the sea
floor. A response surface from a designed experiment. A model's fit measured
over two of its parameters. A model's predictions over a grid of two predictors.
And, through `density`, the shape of a two-dimensional distribution.

A surface is not for data that only *has* three numbers per row. That is a
[3-D scatter](../space.qmd), and the refusal in [One row per
crossing](#one-row-per-crossing) names it for you. Here is the gapminder 2007
table from that section, drawn the way the refusal's message says, with `point`
and `z(population)`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + z(population)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, z is population."*

Each point is a country, and the empty space between two points stands for no
country.
So the question to ask of your own table is whether the space between two of
your samples means anything. On a grid it does; among scattered points it does
not.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a surface takes
and the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("surface")
```

The plots below show every transform a surface takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change. In each one, the sheet is drawn over a floor of cells. `bin` and
`density` cut that floor themselves, and a summary needs `bin` to cut it first.

**Counting.** `bin` and `density` read two continuous positions. `bin` cuts the floor into
cells, and each cell's height is the number of rows inside it. `density`
estimates how closely the rows lie at each place on the floor, and the sheet's
height is that estimate. Neither one takes `z()`, because the transform writes
the height itself. So the sentence needs `space()` to put that height on a third
axis, as [The third geometry of one field](#the-third-geometry-of-one-field)
explains. The left plot draws `surface * bin` on the iris flowers, with
`x(petal_length)`, `y(sepal_length)` and the cube turned 120 degrees. The right
plot is that section's `surface * density`, drawn again here with the same
table, positions and turn, so the two can be compared side by side:

```{r}
((data(iris_flowers) + surface * bin + x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) +
    space(turn = 120) + title("surface * bin")) |
   (data(iris_flowers) + surface * density + x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) +
      space(turn = 120) + title("surface * density"))) +
  theme(height = 430)
```

*"Given the iris flowers: a surface derived by bin, x is petal length, y is
sepal length, in the cube, turned 120, beside a surface derived by density, x is
petal length, y is sepal length, in the cube, turned 120."*

The counts are uneven, because 150 flowers leave most cells with a few rows or
none, and a cell with no rows has no top. The estimate on the right has a value
at every place, so its sheet covers the whole floor.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows of each cell to one value, and
the sheet's height is that value. They need `bin` first, to cut the floor into
cells, so the sentence is `surface * bin * mean` and never `surface * mean`.
They also need `z()` to name the column they reduce. Five plots read the
volcano's `elevation` in the `maunga_whau` table, with `east` on `x` and `north`
on `y`. They give the mean, the median, the highest and the lowest value, and
`quantile(0.9)` gives the elevation that nine tenths of each cell's samples fall
below. `bin(6)` cuts the volcano's floor coarsely, so each cell holds enough
samples for the five to differ. The last plot reads the `gm_all` table, which
holds one row for each country in each of twelve years. It puts `year` on `x`,
`life` on `y` and `population` on `z`, and `bin(12)` cuts its floor. Its `sum`
reads `population`, because people can be added up into a total, and life
expectancies cannot. The table looks like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

```{r}
(((data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(6) * mean + x(east) + y(north) +
     z(elevation, limits = c(90, 200)) + title("surface * bin * mean")) |
    (data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(6) * median + x(east) + y(north) +
       z(elevation, limits = c(90, 200)) + title("surface * bin * median"))) /
   ((data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(6) * max + x(east) + y(north) +
       z(elevation, limits = c(90, 200)) + title("surface * bin * max")) |
      (data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(6) * min + x(east) + y(north) +
         z(elevation, limits = c(90, 200)) + title("surface * bin * min"))) /
   ((data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(6) * quantile(0.9) + x(east) +
       y(north) + z(elevation, limits = c(90, 200)) +
       title("surface * bin * quantile(0.9)")) |
      (data(gm_all) + surface * bin(12) * sum + x(year) + y(life) +
         z(population) + title("surface * bin * sum")))) +
  theme(height = 1100)
```

*"Given Maunga Whau: a surface derived by bin into 6 and mean, x is east, y is
north, z is elevation from 90 to 200, beside a surface derived by bin into 6 and
median, x is east, y is north, z is elevation from 90 to 200; above a surface
derived by bin into 6 and max, x is east, y is north, z is elevation from 90 to
200, beside a surface derived by bin into 6 and min, x is east, y is north, z is
elevation from 90 to 200; above a surface derived by bin into 6 and quantile at
0.9, x is east, y is north, z is elevation from 90 to 200, beside a surface from
all the gapminder years, derived by bin into 12 and sum, x is year, y is life, z
is population."*

Each cube builds its own height axis from its own values. The five volcano plots
all write `limits = c(90, 200)` on `z`, so they share one range, and a height is
the same elevation in each of them. So when the `max` sheet is taller than the
`min` sheet, the elevations really differ. [When each cell holds one
value](#when-each-cell-holds-one-value) explains the plateaus and the vertical
faces between them.

A surface refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. `count` and
`proportion` tally rows into the slots of two categories, and the [3-D
bar](../space.qmd#transforms-in-the-cube) draws one bar in each slot, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses)
shows. `smooth` and `straight` fit a line, and `cumulative` adds a running
total, which [`line`](line.qmd), [`point`](point.qmd) and [`bar`](bar.qmd) draw. The pair
transforms give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`, which
[`interval`](interval.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), [`line`](line.qmd) and [`step`](step.qmd) take. The collision
modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as [`bar`](bar.qmd),
[`point`](point.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd). `partition` is drawn by
[`zone`](zone.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd), and `flow` by
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), [`zone`](zone.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd). `layout`
places a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and
[`edge`](edge.qmd) draw. `cluster` joins the closest categories into a tree,
which [`path`](path.qmd) and [`zone`](zone.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

No column says whether the mesh lines show, or how transparent the whole sheet
is. A setting decides both for the layer without reading any column, and
each mark takes its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a surface's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("surface")
```

A surface is a closed-shape fill, so it takes what a [`bar`](bar.qmd) and a
[`box`](box.qmd) take: a color, an opacity, and a border. `pattern` is the one
fill setting it refuses, and like a `bar` it has no `size`. The next section
says why for both.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

Every flat mark is written with only `x` and `y` as positions, so it is easy to
write a surface that way by mistake. A surface is a sheet through three
positions, so it needs the cube. Leaving out the height and leaving the plot in
the plane are one mistake, not two, so there is one refusal:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north)
```

Its message names both ways to draw in the cube: bind the height to `z`, or let a
transform compute it and add `space()`. It also names the two marks that draw
the field in the plane instead, `zone` as cells and `path` as contours.

A category on either position is the second refusal, for the reason [A
continuous floor](#a-continuous-floor) gave. A face stretches from one sample to
the next, and between two categories there is nothing for it to span. The
sentence below puts `continent` on `x` and `era` on `y`, from the `gm_eras`
table, shown in the same section. `x` and `y` both hold a category, and gog
refuses both, with one message for each:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_eras) + surface + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life)
```

Instead, the message names the [3-D bar](../space.qmd#transforms-in-the-cube),
which draws one bar in each cell two categories make. The refusal above has a
category on both positions. With `year` on `y` instead of `era`, only `x` holds
a category, and gog refuses that one position the same way. `count` and
`proportion` count rows into the cells two categories make. Those cells have
gaps between them and cannot join into one sheet, so a surface refuses both
transforms:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_eras) + surface * count + x(continent) + y(era) + space()
```

That refusal lists the two transforms that do tile a floor, `bin` and
`density`.

`density(levels = )` cuts a field into level *sets*: bands of the plane, each
holding the places between two levels. A surface already uses its third axis for
the estimate, so it has no axis left for a band, and gog refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space()
```

The message names the two marks that draw those bands in the plane:
[`zone`](zone.qmd), which fills them, and `path`, which traces their boundaries.

A sheet can be cut into steps in two ways, and only one of them draws. Cutting
the *floor* into cells is `surface * bin`, which [When each cell holds one
value](#when-each-cell-holds-one-value) draws. Cutting the *height* into bands
is what `levels` asks for, and gog refuses that one. Those bands follow contours
of equal height, not the cells of the floor.

`bandwidth` is a length in one column's own units, and a field spreads over two
columns that measure different quantities. One number cannot be a width in both,
so gog refuses `bandwidth` on every mark that draws a field, a surface included:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space()
```

The message suggests `density(adjust = )` instead. `adjust` is a multiplier with
no unit, so it scales the automatic bandwidth on both axes by the same factor.

There is no `size` on a surface. Its extent is set by the grid it is drawn on,
so a size has nothing left to set, and gog refuses it:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(size = 2)
```

The message says to remove it, or to use a mark that has a size, such as `point`
or `line`.

[`area`](area.qmd) refuses a size for the same reason. A surface also refuses
`pattern`, and it is the only fill mark that does:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")
```

A fill texture is drawn as lines or dots at one spacing on the screen, but each
face of the mesh is seen at its own angle, so the same spacing looks different
on every face. The texture then changes with the viewing angle rather than with
the data, which is the one thing this mark's shading is built to avoid. The
message names what a surface uses instead: slope shading for its shape,
`border_color` for its mesh lines, and `color` for a ramp.

## In short {#in-short}

A surface stretches between neighboring samples, so it needs a floor whose cells
tile. A scatter's table does not give it one. A face needs all four of its
corners, so a missing crossing leaves an opening rather than a guessed height.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A surface needs two continuous positions under it. [Edge](edge.qmd) is the mark
for tables with no column to place on a position: rows naming two things and saying they are
connected.
